headline: Europe says Instagram and Facebook are too addictive

sources.title: Commission preliminarily finds the addictive design of Instagram and Facebook in breach of the Digital Services Act
EU says 'addictive' features on Instagram and Facebook breach its rules
EU puts 'addictive' design of Facebook, Instagram under the DSA microscope
EU tells Meta to change Facebook and Instagram's 'addictive design' | AFP (video, AFP News Agency)

chunks.text: The European Union has {{spoken out}} against two of the world's most popular apps. Officials said that Instagram and Facebook, which are both [[owned by]] the company Meta, are [[designed]] to be too [[addictive]]. They believe the apps break a European law called the Digital Services Act, because their design can [[harm]] users' health and [[well-being]].

verbs.wrong: To start a legal case against someone
verbs.correct: To publicly say what you think
verbs.why: Activists speak out against injustice, and employees sometimes speak out about unsafe conditions at work. Here European officials have spoken out against Instagram and Facebook, saying their designs harm users' health.

chunks.text: The [[regulators]] {{pointed out}} three [[features]] that keep people using the apps [[for hours]]. One feature, called infinite scroll, lets a feed load forever; videos {{start up}} [[on their own]] through [[autoplay]]; and the app keeps {{serving up}} posts it thinks you will like. Together, officials said, these [[tricks]] push the brain into "[[autopilot]]," so users {{end up}} [[scrolling]] without really deciding to.

verbs.correct: To tell someone about a fact or detail
verbs.why: A friend might point out a stain on your shirt, and a teacher can point out a mistake in an essay. European regulators pointed out three addictive features in Instagram and Facebook, including infinite scroll and autoplay.

A car engine can start up on a cold morning, and a computer takes a moment to start up after you press the button. In this story, videos on Instagram and Facebook start up automatically through autoplay, without anyone pressing play.

verbs.wrong: To save something to watch later
verbs.why: Restaurants serve up daily specials, and streaming apps serve up shows based on what you watched before. Here Instagram and Facebook serve up posts and videos the algorithm thinks will keep you scrolling.

verbs.wrong: To lose track of time completely
verbs.correct: To reach a final situation or place
verbs.why: You might end up with the last slice of pizza, or end up in an argument with a stranger. Here small design tricks push users to end up scrolling for hours without ever deciding to.

chunks.text: Europe now wants Meta to {{turn off}} infinite scroll and autoplay [[unless]] a user chooses them, and to {{cut down}} how much the app decides for each person. Meta does not agree. It says it has already {{brought in}} strong rules to protect [[teenagers]], and that the EU's review does not [[fairly]] show the steps it has taken.

verbs.wrong: To make a feature harder to find
verbs.correct: To stop a machine or feature from working
verbs.why: You turn off the lights before bed, and you turn off your phone during a movie. Europe now wants Meta to turn off autoplay and infinite scroll unless a user actively chooses them.

verbs.wrong: To let users make every choice
verbs.correct: To reduce the amount of something
verbs.why: Doctors tell patients to cut down on sugar or cut down on late-night coffee. Europe wants Meta to cut down how much control its algorithm has over what each person sees.

verbs.wrong: To promise stronger rules for the future
verbs.correct: To introduce a new rule, law, or system
verbs.why: Companies bring in new safety rules, and governments bring in fresh laws when problems appear. Meta says it has already brought in strong protections for teenagers, but European regulators are not convinced.

chunks.text: If Meta cannot [[win the argument]], it may have to {{pay out}} a very large [[fine]], [[up to]] 6% of the money it makes around the world each year. The company can still respond before Europe {{hands down}} [[a final decision]] [[in the coming months]]. Many doctors say that [[endless]] scrolling can {{bring on}} [[anxiety]] and [[low moods]] in young people, and some want the apps to {{take away}} these features [[for good]].

verbs.wrong: To lose money because of falling sales
verbs.correct: To pay a large amount of money
verbs.why: Insurance companies pay out after a car accident, and lotteries pay out huge prizes to winners. If Meta loses this case, it may have to pay out a fine worth up to 6 percent of its yearly global revenue.

verbs.wrong: To discuss a decision in private
verbs.correct: To officially give a decision or judgment
verbs.why: Judges hand down prison sentences, and courts hand down rulings that change future cases. Europe has not yet handed down its final decision on Meta, but one is expected in the coming months.

verbs.wrong: To make an illness harder to treat
verbs.correct: To cause something unpleasant to happen
verbs.why: Stress at work can bring on a headache, and cold weather can bring on a nasty cold. Doctors warn that hours of scrolling can bring on anxiety and low moods in young people.

verbs.wrong: To hide a feature from young users
verbs.correct: To remove something and carry it away
verbs.why: Movers take away an old couch, and a storm can take away part of a roof. Some doctors want Instagram and Facebook to take away features like infinite scroll and autoplay for good.

mainIdea.s: European officials say Instagram and Facebook use addictive features like infinite scroll and autoplay. They want Meta to turn these off by default or face a fine.
mainIdea.why: Regulators pointed out three addictive features, and they say Meta must turn them off by default or risk a large fine.

mainIdea.s: European regulators have fined Meta millions of dollars for Instagram and Facebook's design. Meta accepted the ruling and agreed to remove autoplay right away.
mainIdea.why: Close, but no fine has been handed down yet. The article says Meta disagrees and disputes the case.

mainIdea.s: Last year, European regulators opened a separate case against another social media company over young users' personal data. That investigation is still open today.
mainIdea.why: This describes a data privacy case against another company. The article is about the addictive design of Instagram and Facebook.

tf.s: Europe wants Meta to turn off infinite scroll and autoplay by default.
tf.why: Turn off means to stop a feature from working, which is what Europe wants Meta to do unless a user chooses it.

tf.s: The regulators pointed out only one feature that keeps people hooked.
tf.why: The regulators pointed out three features, not one: infinite scroll, autoplay, and personalized posts.

tf.s: Meta agreed at once and brought in all the changes the EU asked for.
tf.why: Meta did not agree; it disputed the findings, so it did not bring in, or introduce, the changes.

tf.s: The European Union spoke out against Instagram and Facebook's design.
tf.why: Speak out means to publicly say what you think, which the EU did against the two apps.

tf.s: If Meta loses, it could pay out up to 6% of its yearly global revenue.
tf.why: Pay out means to pay a large amount, and the fine could reach 6% of Meta's yearly revenue.

tf.s: Doctors say that endless scrolling helps take away anxiety in young people.
tf.why: Doctors warn that scrolling can bring on, or cause, anxiety; it does not take it away.
